en: The *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*,
one fascicle;
compiled and brought forth by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Changgan Monastery during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Preaching the Dharma “Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!
Of the winter month, one night has passed and one night remains; three months are yet to come. Old age and death are drawing near, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.”
Chapter Two: On Exhortation and Instruction. "Venerable sirs!
For the sake of attaining the Path, you must practice with single-minded diligence and vigor. Why is this?"
"Because all Buddhas diligently applied themselves with single-minded vigor, they attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; how much more so for other dharmas of the wholesome path!
Chapter Three: The Assembly. "Those who had not yet received full ordination have already departed."
“The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what should we do first?
One person replied:
“We shall perform the Poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa.”
“Venerable sirs!
Those bhikṣuṇīs who have not arrived should announce their *chanda* (consent) and purification.
Chapter Four: Chapter on Offerings Joining the ten fingers and palms together, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas.
I now wish to recite the precepts; the Saṃgha should listen with a single mind.
Even regarding minor offenses, one’s heart should feel great dread;
having committed an offense, repent with a single mind, and do not commit it again hereafter.
The horse of the mind gallops down evil paths; heedlessness is difficult to restrain.
The Buddha taught the practice of earnest precepts, which are like sharp reins and bits.
When the Buddha’s mouth utters instructions and admonitions, those who are virtuous are able to believe and accept them.
This person has a well-trained horse that can destroy the army of afflictions.
If one does not accept instruction nor cherish the precepts,
this person’s horse is untamed and sinks into the army of afflictions.
If a person guards the precepts as a yak cherishes its tail,
and binds the mind with heedfulness as a monkey is bound by chains;
if they are constantly diligent day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom;
Such a person, within the Buddha-dharma, Is able to attain a pure livelihood.
Chapter Five: Harmonizing the Assembly “Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!

Today is the fifteenth day of the *poṣadha*; we shall recite the *Prātimokṣa*. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, may the Saṃgha with one mind perform the *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
"Thus it is announced.
Chapter Six: Purifying the Assembly. "Venerable sirs!
Now we shall together perform the *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*. May the Saṃgha listen with a single mind!"
"Those who have committed an offense should confess; those who are free from offense should remain silent.
By remaining silent, it shall be known that the Venerable Ones are pure.
Just as this was asked and answered by each individual bhikṣuṇī, so too was it proclaimed three times within the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs.

If there is a bhikṣuṇī who, when the third proclamation has been made within such an assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, remembers having committed an offense but does not disclose it, she incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Venerable sirs!
The Buddha has declared that the offense of intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the path.
If a bhikṣuṇī seeks purity within this regard, she should confess any offense she remembers; by confessing it, she will find peace, but by not confessing it, her offense becomes increasingly grave.
“Venerable sirs! The introduction to the Prātimokṣa has been recited. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard?
He asks a second and a third time in the same manner.
"Is there purity herein? "Venerable sirs!
There is purity herein, for we are silent; thus shall this matter be held."
“Venerable sirs!
These eight *pārājika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*.

If a bhikṣuṇī, having entered into the training of the bhikṣuṇīs, does not relinquish the precepts, nor confess her weakness in observing them, yet commits sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense and should not live in community with the others.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given—this is called stealing property.
Because she has taken what was not given, if a king or one equal to a king should seize her, or kill her, or bind her, or banish her, or impose a fine upon her, or say:
'You little child!'"
"You thief! You fool!"—
if a bhikṣuṇī takes an object in such a manner without it being given to her, she commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with the others.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of a human or one who resembles a human with her own hand, or provides a knife, or instructs them to die, or praises death, saying:
'What is the use of living such a wretched life?'"
"Death is better than life.

Following that person's inclination toward death, she teaches them to die and praises death through various causes and conditions. If that person dies as a result of these actions, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communal residence with the Saṃgha.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, not knowing and not seeing, being empty and devoid of superhuman qualities, says of herself:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"

If, at a later time, whether questioned or not, this bhikṣuṇī—out of greed for gain and honor—speaks what she does not know as if she knows it, or speaks what she has not seen as if she has seen it, uttering empty, deceptive, and false words—with the exception of overweening pride—this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with others.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with lustful intent, listens to a man with lustful intent, and—below the hairline and above the knees or wrists—has him pull back her robe and then rub her body with or against the grain, pull or push her, press or pinch her, or embrace her from above or below, this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense; she is not to live in community."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, listens to a man with a lustful mind, and allows him to take her hand or take hold of her robe, stands together with him, speaks together with him, makes an appointment to enter a secluded place, waits for the man to come, and behaves toward his body as a laywoman would—[this is an offense]."
By these eight matters, the signs of greedy attachment are shown; such a bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not dwell together [with the Saṃgha].

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, conceals it for even a single night, and later—whether that bhikṣuṇī has fallen away, remains, ceased, or departed—says this:
'I also previously knew that this bhikṣuṇī had committed such and such an offense, but I did not wish to report it myself, nor did I wish to speak of it to the Saṃgha.'"
Or if someone says:
"How can a younger sister defile her elder sister?
that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with the others.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣu has been lawfully subjected to a formal act of suspension for refusal to see an offense by a united Saṃgha acting with one mind—being alone without a second, without companion or partner, and neither ceasing nor resting—and yet goes to follow him in compliance; [she commits an offense]."
The bhikṣuṇīs should thus admonish that bhikṣuṇī:

"This bhikṣu is a member of the unified Saṃgha who has been lawfully subjected to the formal act of *ajñapti* for not seeing [his offense]; he is solitary, without a second, without companion or partner, and does not cease or desist. You must not follow this bhikṣu."

When the bhikṣuṇīs have thus admonished her and she persists in this matter without relinquishing it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time in order to make her relinquish that matter.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not be allowed to dwell in communion.
"Venerable sirs!
The eight *pārājika* rules have been recited. If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these rules, that bhikṣuṇī is not permitted to dwell together [with the community] nor to engage in communal affairs."
As it was before, so it is now; this bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense and should not dwell together with the community.
Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
A second and third time he asked in the same manner:
"Is there purity in this matter?
"Venerable sirs! [We are pure]."
"In this matter, we are pure; because we remain silent, let it be so held.
"Venerable sirs!
These seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*."

"If a bhikṣuṇī practices the art of matchmaking—whether conveying a man's intent to a woman, or a woman's intent to a man; whether for the purpose of marriage or for illicit liaison—even for as long as a single meeting—this offense is a saṃghāvaśeṣa, which is to be confessed upon its first commission."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of malice and anger, should defame a bhikṣuṇī who is free from a pārājika offense by means of a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy her holy life."

If, at a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣuṇī knows that the matter was groundless and yet spoke these words out of malice, this constitutes an initial offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* which must be confessed.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of malice and anger, takes up a matter that is unrelated or resembles a partial fact, and slanders another bhikṣuṇī with a charge of a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy that bhikṣuṇī's holy life."

If, at a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣuṇī knows this matter to be merely a semblance of a partial offense, yet speaks these words out of malice, this constitutes an initial offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* which is to be confessed.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind affected by leakage, takes food directly from the hand of a man whose mind is also affected by leakage, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa, which is to be confessed, committed upon the first instance."
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
'If you, with a mind free from outflows, take food with your own hands from a man whose mind is subject to outflows and eat it, or use it as you please, what power do you have over that?'"
"This rule is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, subject to confession, committed upon the first transgression.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether by night or by day, in a different village or in a different boundary, should spend the night alone across the water on the further shore, this rule is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, subject to confession, committed upon the first transgression."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, relying on her influence, speaks ill of others, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa, involving confession, which constitutes an initial transgression.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman is a thief who has been sentenced to death, and knowing that the king and the authorities have not granted pardon, yet admits her as a disciple, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa, involving confession, which constitutes an initial transgression."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has been lawfully subjected to a formal act of suspension for refusal to see an offense by a harmonious Saṃgha, neither consults the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha nor obtains their consent (*chanda*), and then goes outside the boundary to grant the lifting of that suspension—this action constitutes an initial offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* that must be confessed. "If a bhikṣuṇī desires to break a harmonious Saṃgha and diligently applies herself to the means of maintaining such schism..."
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her thus:

"Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha by diligently employing means to uphold the matter of schism. You should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha; for when the Saṃgha is in harmony, it dwells in joy and without contention, with one mind and one training like water and milk mixed together, attaining peaceful and happy abiding."
"You should abandon this pursuit of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣuṇīs have thus admonished her, if she persists in this matter and does not abandon it, they should admonish her a second and third time to abandon it.
If she desists after being admonished two or three times, it is well;
if she does not desist, this matter reaches the third [admonition], and she commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that must be confessed.
"If a bhikṣuṇī seeks to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, and there are other like-minded bhikṣuṇīs who assist her—whether one, two, or many—and they speak to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:"
"In this matter, do not speak ill of this bhikṣuṇī. Why is that?
This bhikṣuṇī teaches the Dharma and teaches the Vinaya; she does not teach what is not the Dharma, nor does she teach what is not the Vinaya."
"Whatever this bhikṣuṇī has said is exactly what we desire; she speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge.
Whatever this bhikṣuṇī has said is precisely what we desire, delight in, and accept."
The bhikṣuṇīs should thus admonish those bhikṣuṇīs who support them:
"Do not speak these words:
'This bhikṣuṇī speaks the Dharma and speaks the Vinaya; she does not speak what is non-Dharma or what is non-Vinaya.'"
"Whatever this bhikṣuṇī has said is exactly what we desire; she speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge.
Whatever this bhikṣuṇī has said is precisely what we desire, delight in, and accept."
"Do not assist in seeking to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead assist in bringing about harmony in the Saṃgha.
When the Saṃgha is in harmony, it dwells in joy and without dispute, with a single mind and a single training, like water and milk mixed together, attaining a state of peaceful abiding."

"When the bhikṣuṇīs have thus admonished her, if she persists in this matter and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs shall admonish her a second and third time so that she may relinquish this matter."
If she abandons [the course] after being admonished two or three times, it is well.
If she does not abandon it, this matter reaches the third [admonition], and she commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, in whatever village she relies upon for residence, engages in evil conduct and defiles the families of others, such that she is seen by all, heard by all, and known by all."
The bhikṣuṇīs should speak thus:
"You have committed evil conduct and defiled other families; this has been seen by all, heard by all, and known by all. You must depart; you should not remain here."
That bhikṣuṇī said to the other bhikṣuṇīs:
"The bhikṣuṇīs act out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of fear, and out of delusion."
"Why is this? Among bhikṣuṇīs who have committed such identical offenses, some are expelled while others are not.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Do not speak these words:
'The bhikṣuṇīs act out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of fear, or out of delusion.
For what reason? [Because it is not so. "
The bhikṣuṇīs do not act out of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion.
You have committed evil conduct and defiled families; this has been seen, heard, and known by all. You must abandon such speech that follows favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion.
"You all should leave; you ought not to remain here.
When he has been admonished in this manner, if he does not relinquish that matter, he should be admonished a second and a third time so that he may relinquish it.
If she relinquishes [the offense] when admonished up to three times, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and must be confessed.

"There was a bhikṣuṇī of evil character and perverse speech; when the other bhikṣuṇīs spoke to her concerning matters that were in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as found in the Sūtras, this bhikṣuṇī spoke perversely and would not accept [their words], saying to the bhikṣuṇīs:"
"Do not speak of my faults or virtues, nor shall I speak of yours.
The bhikṣuṇīs should say to her:
"The bhikṣuṇīs speak in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the contents of the Śīla-sūtra; do not speak perversely, but speak in conformity."
The bhikṣuṇīs shall speak to you in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and you, in turn, shall speak to the bhikṣuṇīs in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. Why is this?
In this way, the assembly of all Tathāgatas will attain increased benefit, because they instruct one another through mutual discourse and emerge together from transgressions.
You should therefore abandon such perverse speech.

"When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner and she persists in this matter and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time so that she may relinquish this matter."
If she desists when admonished two or three times, it is well;
if she does not desist, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that must be confessed.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while engaged in a quarrel with another bhikṣuṇī, speaks as follows:"

"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha, and I renounce the precepts. It is not only the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who know the Way; there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame and propriety and delight in upholding the precepts. I shall practice the holy life under them."
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Do not quarrel with the bhikṣuṇīs and say such things as:

'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha, and I renounce the precepts. It is not only the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who know the Way; there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame, are virtuous, and delight in upholding the precepts; I shall practice the holy life under them.'"
"You should take delight in practicing the holy life within the Buddha’s Dharma, and you must abandon this mind of personal aversion.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have offered such admonitions and she still persists in her stance and does not relinquish it, they should admonish her a second and third time in order to cause her to relinquish that matter.
If she desists when admonished a second and third time, it is well;
if she does not desist, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense requiring confession.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while engaged in a quarrel with another bhikṣuṇī, speaks as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī acts out of favoritism, acts out of hatred, acts out of fear, or acts out of delusion," the other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her thus:
"Do not speak these words while quarreling with the bhikṣuṇīs:
[that the Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs acts out of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion]."
“The community of bhikṣuṇīs acts out of attachment, acts out of aversion, acts out of fear, and acts out of delusion.
Why is this? Because the community of bhikṣuṇīs does not act out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion.
"You should abandon these words spoken out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner and she persists in her position without relinquishing it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time, so that she may relinquish this matter.
If she abandons [the course] after being admonished a second or third time, it is well;
if she does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that must be confessed.
"If two bhikṣuṇīs, with one mind, together commit an evil deed, incur an evil reputation, harass the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and mutually conceal their offenses..."
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish them thus:
"You must not, with one mind, collectively commit evil deeds, incur an evil reputation, harass the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs, and conceal each other's offenses."
"You should each practice in separation; practicing in separation increases the Buddha-dharma.
You must abandon this compliance with unwholesome conduct.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have been admonished in this manner, if they persist in their position and do not relinquish it, they should be admonished a second and third time in order to cause them to relinquish that matter.
If she relinquishes [the course] when admonished a second and third time, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense requiring confession.
"If a bhikṣuṇī instructs two bhikṣuṇīs, saying:..."
"Do not practice in separation; you should practice with a unified mind.
Those who practice in separation do not achieve growth, whereas those who practice with a unified mind do indeed achieve growth."
“Among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are others just like you; it was because of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to practice separation.
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her in this way:
“Do not instruct two bhikṣuṇīs to speak as follows:”
“You all should not practice in separation; you should practice with a unified mind.
Those who practice in separation cannot increase the Buddha-dharma, whereas those who practice with a unified mind can indeed increase it.”
“There are others among the community who are just like you; it was because of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to practice separately.
You should abandon this practice of encouraging improper conduct.
When the bhikṣuṇīs admonish them in this manner, if they persist in their position and do not relinquish it, they should be admonished a second and third time so that they may abandon such matters.
"If, after being admonished a second and third time, he relinquishes it, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for which one must confess. "Venerable sirs!"
The seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas have already been explained: nine are offenses by the very first commission, and eight require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these offenses, she must undergo *mānatva* for half a month within both divisions of the Saṃgha to satisfy the minds of both divisions of the Saṃgha.
Each of the two divisions of the Saṃgha must consist of twenty members to expel this bhikṣuṇī’s offense.

If there is even one person missing from either of the two divisions, the bhikṣuṇī’s offense is not considered expelled; the two divisions of the Saṃgha may be censured, for such is the proper rule of this Dharma.
"Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
He asks a second and a third time in the same way:
"Are you pure in this matter?"
“Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.
Venerable sirs!”
These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished making her robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina*, keeps an extra robe, she may do so for up to ten days."
If one keeps them beyond this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. "If a bhikṣuṇī,
having finished her robes and cast off the *kaṭhina* cloth, should be separated from any one of her five robes for even a single night, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*,
except by formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*) of the Saṃgha."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and discarded the kaṭhina cloth, should obtain an out-of-season robe, that bhikṣuṇī, if she requires it, may take it with her own hand and must quickly have it made up and formally accepted."
If it is sufficient, that is well;
if it is insufficient, one may keep this robe for up to one month in order to hope for further robes so as to make it complete.
Should one keep it beyond this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī asks for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative,
and she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
except in cases of special circumstances."

Regarding the "causes and conditions": being deprived of one's robes, having one's robes lost, having one's robes burned, or having one's robes carried away by water—these are called the causes and conditions.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when her robes have been taken away, lost, burned, or carried away by water, should beg for robes from a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative, and they should offer her many robes at their own discretion, that bhikṣuṇī may accept only a set of upper and lower robes."
If one accepts more than this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If, for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative prepares the price for a robe and says:
'With this price for a robe, I shall buy such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣuṇī.'"
If this bhikṣuṇī, without having been previously invited by a formal request, goes to the place of a layman or a laywoman and speaks with agreement, saying:
"Prepare such an amount for the price of cloth for me, and buy such and such a garment for me, so that it may be of good quality."
If she should obtain the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If, for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, two unrelated laymen (*gṛhapati*) and their wives each prepare the price for a robe and say:
'With this price for a robe, we shall each purchase such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣuṇī.'"
If this bhikṣuṇī, without having been previously invited by personal choice, goes to the place of a layman or a householder’s wife and speaks with agreement, saying:
"Each of you should prepare the price for a robe; together we shall make one robe to give to me, so that it may be of good quality."
If she should obtain the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If, for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, a king, a royal minister, a brāhmaṇa, or a householder sends a messenger to deliver the value of a robe..."
The messenger went to where the bhikṣuṇī was and said:
"Venerable One!
So-and-so has sent this value for robes; you should accept it."
The bhikṣuṇī should say:
"It is not in accordance with the dharma for me, a bhikṣuṇī, to accept the price of a robe.
If at the time when I need a robe I obtain a pure robe, I shall receive it with my own hands and quickly make it into a robe to wear."
The messenger should say to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Venerable lady,
is there an attendant who can perform services for you, a bhikṣuṇī?"
That bhikṣuṇī should point out an attendant, whether a monastery servant or an upāsaka, who is capable of serving as an attendant for the bhikṣuṇīs.
He sent a messenger to the person in charge of the goods, saying:
"Take this money for robes and have a robe made in such a manner; give it to that bhikṣuṇī. When that bhikṣuṇī comes needing a robe, you should give her the robe."
Having spoken thus, the messenger returned and reported to the bhikṣuṇī:
"I have finished speaking,
O Venerable One!"
"When you need robes, go and fetch them; we shall give you robes.
That bhikṣuṇī went to the place where the attendants were and requested robes, saying:
"I need robes."
If he repeats this request up to two or three times and receives the robe, that is well;
if he does not receive it, he should go before the attendant and stand in silence for four or even six times.
If he stands silently for four times up to six times and obtains the robe, it is well;
if he does not obtain the robe and seeks it beyond that number of times and obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go to the place where the value of the robe was sent from, either going himself or sending a messenger, and say:
"I did not receive the value of the robe you sent; you yourself must take care of your property so that it is not lost. This is how it should be done.
"If a bhikṣuṇī takes treasure with her own hand, or causes another to take it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes various uses of treasure, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī’s bowl, which is in use and has fewer than five repairs, is broken and she asks for a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.”
This bowl should be relinquished among the community of bhikṣuṇīs; the lowest bowl in that assembly should be given to this bhikṣuṇī, and she should be instructed as follows: "O bhikṣuṇī!..."
"One should maintain this bowl until it breaks; such is the proper course.
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If, for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative has a weaver weave a robe, and that bhikṣuṇī, having not been previously invited, goes to the weaver and says:
'Do you know [this]? "
"This robe has been woven for my sake; weave it well, weave it very well, weave it wide, and weave it clean, and I shall give you some extra payment.
If that bhikṣuṇī, whether speaking herself or sending someone else to speak, later provides food or the price of food for the sake of obtaining a fine garment.
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives a robe to another bhikṣuṇī and later, out of anger and resentment, takes it back herself or causes someone else to take it back, saying:
'Give me my robe back; I will not give it to you.'"
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, receives an urgent gift of a robe, and that bhikṣuṇī has need of this robe, she may take it with her own hand and keep it until the time of the *pravāraṇā*."
If one keeps more than this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, seeks it for herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī is ill, she is permitted to take four kinds of medicinal substances for internal consumption—
ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar— and may keep them overnight and consume them for up to seven days."
If one keeps it beyond this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra bowl for even a single night;
if she keeps it beyond this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a timely robe into an untimely robe-portion, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes an untimely robe into a timely robe-portion, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having traded robes with another bhikṣuṇī, later goes to that bhikṣuṇī's place and says:
'I am returning your robe to you; you must return my robe to me.'"
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If, for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, many unrelated laymen and laywomen each provide the price for a robe and say:
'We shall each purchase such a robe with this price and give it to a certain bhikṣuṇī.'"
"Suppose this bhikṣuṇī, having not been previously invited, later goes to the place of many laymen and laywomen and says to them:
'You all should use these funds for clothing to purchase such a garment together and give it to me, for the sake of its excellence.'"
If one obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī begs for gold or silver for herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having requested this, further seeks something else, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī requests something for the sake of the Saṃgha, yet uses it for another purpose, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī begs for something for her own sake and uses it for another purpose, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī begs for something for the sake of many people and uses it for another purpose, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī requests a heavy robe, she should request one worth four *kārsāpaṇas*.
To request more than this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests a light robe, she should request one worth two and a half *kārsāpaṇas*."
"To beg for more than this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. "Venerable sirs!
The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules have been recited. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in regard to these?"
A second and third time he asked in the same manner:
"Is there purity in this matter?
"Venerable sirs!"
"In this matter we are pure; because we are silent, let it be so held.
"Venerable sirs, these one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally speaks falsehoods, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī compares her physical appearance with that of another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī engages in double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, after a dispute has been settled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, raises it again, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī teaches the dharma by means of phrases to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, possessing a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika,
except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha."
"If a bhikṣuṇī first encourages [others] to give, and later says:
'The bhikṣuṇīs have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal intimacy,' it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, should say:
‘What is the use of these minor,琐碎 (trifling) precepts?
When they are recited every half-month, they cause the bhikṣuṇīs to feel doubt, regret, distress, anxiety, and unhappiness, giving rise to a mind that turns away from the precepts.’”
If one thus disparages the precepts, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī cuts down or fells a "village of spirits" or a "village of seeds," it is a pāyattika.
10. "If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, reviles a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, under false pretenses, silently harasses another, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī spreads out monastic bedding—coarse or fine rope beds, blankets, or quilts—on an open space, whether she spreads them herself or causes others to do so, and sits or lies upon them, yet when departing does not herself remove them nor instruct others to remove them, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī spreads out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha in a bhikṣuṇī’s dwelling, or causes another to spread it,
and sits or lies upon it, yet upon departing does not herself remove it nor instruct another to remove it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure within a bhikṣuṇī's dwelling, drags herself out or causes another to drag her out, saying:
'You foolish woman, go far away!'"
"One should not dwell upon this," [otherwise] it is a pāyattika,
except in special circumstances.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has already spread bedding within a bhikṣuṇī’s dwelling, later comes and forcibly spreads her own, or causes someone else to spread it, saying:
'If you do not wish for this, you should leave of your own accord.'"
...is a *pāyattika*, except when there is a specific cause.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, in a multi-storied building within a bhikṣuṇī’s dwelling, sits or lies down with force upon a chair or bed with pointed legs, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living beings, uses it herself to sprinkle on grass or mix with mud, or causes another to do so, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī sits alone with a single bhikṣu in a secluded, concealed place, it is a pāyattika."
20. “If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, stays in a ‘house of merit’ (puṇya-śālā) for more than one meal, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the home of a layperson and they freely invite her, giving much cake and parched grain, the bhikṣuṇīs who require them should take two or three bowls.”
If one takes more than this, it is a pāyattika offense.
Having taken two or three bowls, one should go outside and share them with other bhikṣuṇīs; this is the proper rule.
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika, except for specific causes. The causes are:
when one is ill, when making robes, when traveling on a road, when traveling by boat, when a great assembly has gathered, and when invited by a śramaṇa."
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats leftover food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī places food that has not been formally offered into her mouth, it is a pāyattika,
except for water and tooth-sticks.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that water contains insects and takes it for use, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī sits down forcefully in a house where food is being served, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī sits down alone with a single man inside a house where food is being served, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives food with her own hands to a naked ascetic, or to a male or female renunciant, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally goes to view an army on its march, it is a pāyattika,
except when there is a valid reason."
30. “If a bhikṣuṇī, having a reason, stays overnight in an army for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, while staying overnight in an army for two nights, goes to look at military formations, weapons, ensigns, banners, or the battle between two armies, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, raises her hand toward another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, conceals it for even a single night, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
‘Come, let us go together to various households.’”
That bhikṣuṇī, instead of instructing her to give food, spoke these words:
"Go away! I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone."
If, with the intent to annoy another, one acts through such causes and conditions, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, lights a fire in the open air—whether of grass, wood, cow dung, tree bark, or refuse—whether lighting it herself or causing another to light it, it is an offense of expiation."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having given her consent for a formal monastic act in accordance with the Dharma, later regrets it and says,
'I should not have given it,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight in the same room as a person who has not received full ordination for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus:
'I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma in this way: practicing the dharmas that obstruct the path does not actually obstruct the path.'"
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her in this way:
"Do not speak such words as:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma; practicing the dharmas that obstruct the path does not actually obstruct the path.'"
"Do not misrepresent the Buddha; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Buddha.
The Buddha does not speak such words. Through various causes and conditions, the Buddha has taught that the factors obstructing the path are indeed capable of obstructing the path."
"You should abandon this evil and false view.
When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner and she persists in holding to it and refuses to abandon it, they should admonish her a second and a third time to make her abandon that matter.
If she desists after being admonished two or three times, it is well;
if she does not desist, it is a pāyattika.
Forty: "If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has spoken thus, yet does not repent in accordance with the Dharma and does not abandon her evil and false views..."
If one associates with, dwells with, or shares a room with a person who has been expelled according to the Dharma, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a śrāmaṇerikā should speak thus:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma; practicing sexual intercourse cannot obstruct the Path.'"
The bhikṣuṇīs should instruct her thus:
"Do not speak these words:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; practicing sexual desire cannot obstruct the path.'"
"Do not slander the Buddha; to slander the Buddha is unwholesome.
The Buddha does not speak such words. Through various causes and conditions, the Buddha has taught that sensual desire can obstruct the path."
"You should abandon this evil, false view.

When the bhikṣuṇīs instruct them in this manner, if they persist in holding to this matter and do not relinquish it, they should be instructed up to three times to cause them to relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes [the practice] when instructed thus a second and third time, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should speak to her as follows:
"O śrāmaṇerī, from this day forward you should not say:..."
"The Buddha is my teacher.
Furthermore, you should not follow behind the bhikṣuṇīs.
While other śrāmaṇerikās are permitted to stay two nights in the same room as bhikṣuṇīs, you are not permitted to do so now.
"Foolish woman, go away!
You should not remain here.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a śrāmaṇerī has been thus expelled, nevertheless keeps her, provides for her, shares tasks with her, or sleeps with her, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether it be precious objects or things resembling precious objects, takes them up herself or causes another to take them up, it is a pāyattika, except in cases of necessity.
'Cases of necessity' refers to when precious objects or things resembling precious objects are within a monastery or within a dwelling, and she takes them with this thought:"
"The master shall return when he comes.
This matter should be handled accordingly.
"If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe, she should use one of three colors to disfigure the color of that robe: [blue, black, or madder]."
Whether it be blue, mud-colored, or madder-red.
If a bhikṣuṇī wears new robes without having dyed them with one of these three colors of ruin, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī bathes less than once every half-month, it is a pāyattika."
Except for special circumstances.

Special circumstances refer to: the remaining one month and a half of spring, the first month of summer—these two months and a half; times of extreme heat, illness, wind, rain, manual labor, or travel. These are called special circumstances.
“If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally causes another bhikṣuṇī to feel doubt or regret, making her mind uneasy for even a moment, and for this reason there is no other [intention], it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī tickles another with her fingers, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī plays in the water, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a man, it is a pāyattika.
Fifty: "If a bhikṣuṇī herself terrifies another bhikṣuṇī, or causes another to terrify her—even if done in jest—it is a pāyattika."

“If a bhikṣuṇī herself hides a bhikṣuṇī’s robes, bowl, door-bolt, leather sandals, needle-case, or various other articles belonging to her according to the Dharma, or causes another to hide them—even in jest—it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and they do not return it, she forcibly takes it back; this is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, with groundless charges of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, slanders another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment with a man to travel together on the same road as far as a village, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī travels along the same road with a thief, even as far as a single village, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth with her own hand, or instructs another to dig it, saying:
‘Dig here,’ [it is a pāyattika].”
“An offense of expiation (pāyattika).
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation for the four-month *pravāraṇā*, and accepts beyond this period, it is an offense of expiation;
except in the case of a regular invitation, a repeated invitation, or a special invitation.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, should say:
'I will not train in these precepts; first I must ask other bhikṣus who are holders of the Sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā.'"
This is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to know this rule, she should train in it from this precept; she should ask other bhikṣus who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās. She should ask them thus:
"What is the meaning of these words?"
"This matter should be handled thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, after having quarreled with another bhikṣuṇī, secretly goes to stand by and listen [thinking], "I shall remember what that bhikṣuṇī says," [she commits an offense]. "
Pāyattika. Sixty: "If a bhikṣuṇī rises and leaves in silence while the Saṃgha is conducting its business, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī is disrespectful, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika,
except in cases of urgent necessity.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having accepted an invitation for the Saṃgha, goes to another house before or after the midday meal, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the palace of a consecrated Kṣatriya king at night when the night has not yet passed and the treasures have not yet been stored away, and she crosses the threshold or the place of the threshold, it is a pāyattika;
except in cases of urgent necessity."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the precepts are being recited, should say:
'I only now learn that this matter has been included in the Sūtra of the Precepts and is recited every half-month.'"
If the other bhikṣuṇīs know that this bhikṣuṇī has already heard this precept being recited two or three times before, how much more so if it has been recited even more than that!
This bhikṣuṇī cannot escape by claiming ignorance; she must be made to repent according to the Dharma for the offense committed, and she must be rebuked until she feels weary of her conduct:
"You have lost what is beneficial; this is evil and unwholesome."
"When you were reciting the precepts, you did not respect the precepts nor listen with a single-minded focus.
On account of this matter, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a needle case from bone, tooth, or horn, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to have a bed made, it must be made according to the prescribed measurement: the legs shall be eight finger-breadths high, excluding the space for the mortises.
Should she have one made exceeding this, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself fills a bedding item with cotton-wool, or causes another to fill it, it is a pāyattika.
Seventy: If a bhikṣuṇī makes a robe according to the measurement of the Buddha’s robes, or makes one that exceeds it, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the measurement of a Buddha’s robe: it is nine spans long and six spans wide; this is the measurement of a Buddha’s robe.
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats raw or cooked garlic, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair of the private parts [the anus or the vulva], it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, while washing, inserts her finger into the female organ beyond two finger-joints, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī slaps her female organ with her palm, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī cooks raw food to make a meal, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī stands waiting in front of a bhikṣu while he is eating, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī throws excrement or urine outside a wall, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī discards excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands or converses in private with a single bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
80. “If a bhikṣuṇī stands together alone with a single bhikṣu in an open space and converses with him, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī stands together alone with a single layman in a secluded place and converses with him, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands or converses alone with a single layman in an open space, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī stands or sits with a man in the dark without a lamp, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī inserts her male organ into a female organ, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
'Come, virtuous lady!'"
"Stay in my room with me.
Later, becoming angry and displeased, he either drags her out himself or orders someone else to drag her out, saying:
"Get far away and perish!"
"Do not dwell in this.
For these reasons, there is no difference [in the offense], and it is a *pāyattika*.
"If two bhikṣuṇīs lie together on one bed, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If two bhikṣuṇīs lie down together on a single bedding, it is a pāyattika.
If two bhikṣuṇīs lie down covered by a single garment, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and stands together with, speaks with, or converses in private with a single bhikṣu—having sent away a bhikṣuṇī who accompanies her for the sake of seeking a secluded opportunity—it is a pāyattika."

90. “If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and stands together with, speaks with, or converses in secret with a single layman, and she sends away another bhikṣuṇī wishing to speak alone [with him], it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, quarreling and being angry with another bhikṣuṇī, strikes her own body and weeps, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, while quarreling with another bhikṣuṇī, performs incantations for sorcery or incantations for hell, it is a pāyattika."

“Desiring a virtuous mind, do not be negligent; One should diligently train in the noble Dharma.”
"If there be one who knows how to dwell in silent single-mindedness, Then they shall no longer have sorrow or affliction.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa Buddha, surrounded by twenty thousand bhikṣus, spoke this precept-sūtra:
"Do no evil whatsoever; One should fully cultivate wholesome dharmas."
"Purify your own will and intention; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Thus did the Tathāgata Śākyamuni Buddha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—surrounded by a thousand two hundred and fifty monks who had never before attained such a state—proclaim this precept-sūtra:
"To guard the body is excellent; to guard the speech is also excellent."
To guard the mind is good; to guard all [the senses] is also good.
A bhikṣu who guards all [the senses] shall be freed from all suffering.
A bhikṣu who restrains his speech and mind, and whose body commits no evil, [attains this state].
These three paths of action are pure; one attains the path realized by the noble ones.
If a person strikes or reviles you, do not retaliate; toward those who harbor resentment, let your heart feel no resentment;
toward those who are angry, let your mind always remain pure; seeing others commit evil, do not do it yourself.
“The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who are able to rescue and protect the world—
The precept sūtra they have taught, I have now fully expounded.”
The Buddhas and their disciples revere this Sūtra of Precepts;
having revered the Sūtra of Precepts, they each revere one another.
Endowed with shame and remorse, they are able to attain the unconditioned Way.
"Venerable sirs!
The Prātimokṣa has been recited; the Saṃgha, being of one mind, has performed the Poṣadha.
*The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Sarvāstivādins, in one fascicle.*
